statement: The next topic is separation of concerns, introduced by asking the class what the schema of Instagram's post table would look like and what it would store.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Separation of concern is what I want to discuss next. Now, this is a very interesting concept.

statement: A student's proposed post table stores the user ID of the poster, the post content (text/caption) and when it was created (created_at); the teacher accepts these columns.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Yeah, so it will have a user ID posted. Then it will have the post content like the text, post text, caption.

statement: A student proposed storing tags in the post table; the teacher corrected that on Instagram tags are not explicit fields - hashtags are part of the caption.
detail: The same point is repeated later in the hashtag service: there is no special hashtag column, hashtags live in the caption.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: It's not explicit tags. It's part of the caption.

statement: A student proposed storing the photo's URL - the pre-signed URL obtained during upload - in the post table.
detail: Teacher: not the pre-signed URL but 'the actual CDN URL' is what people would store - and he then uses this to show that storing any URL at all is suboptimal (derivable values should not be stored).
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So it will be like the URL of the photo which you got, the pre-signed URL.
flags: check: speaker - "Yeah, basically, yeah" may be Student 2

statement: In every cohort, almost everyone designs the post table with an image URL column; the teacher calls this suboptimal (saying 'wrong' would be too strong).
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every single cohort, every single person thinks of it building. But no, this is wrong. Why? This is suboptimal.

statement: If something is derivable, do not store it - store the crux information and derive the rest when needed.
detail: Repeated at 01:12:50 ('I should put it in my t-shirt'): not storing the derived value gives the flexibility to switch the CDN whenever you want or point directly to S3, and makes life simple. The teacher calls it a really important point.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Always, always, always, always remember that if something is derivable, don't store it.

statement: The naive post table has a post ID, the user who created the post and an image URL; the natural follow-up is which URL to store - the S3 URL or the CDN URL - and the naive answer is the CDN URL because images are served via the CDN.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now post, I'll have a post ID. I'll have user who created a post and I'll have image URL.

statement: Instagram most probably used Cloudflare as its CDN; after Facebook acquired it, it could no longer use Cloudflare and had to use the Facebook CDN - with stored URLs that would mean going through the entire database and changing the image URL of every single post.
detail: Teacher hedges ('most probably'). Later (01:23:21) he points at fbcdn.net in a live Instagram URL: 'They were using Cloudflare, they migrated to FBCDN.'
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Most probably they were using Cloudflare as a CDN. Facebook came and acquired them, but now they cannot use Cloudflare CDN.

statement: Storing the S3 URL instead of the CDN URL is no better: you may have to change cloud provider, e.g. if Amazon shoots up its pricing by 4x there is little you can do.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if I store S3 URL? What if you change your cloud provider?

statement: Microsoft changed the billing of its Bing APIs, making every API call 4 to 10x more costly because everyone had started using Bing - 'the world works on money'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Microsoft changed their billing of Bing APIs, right?

statement: Structure your system so that you are not binding yourself to any one vendor or provider.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you always have to ensure the way you are structuring your system, you are not binding yourself to something.

statement: In the post table, keep URL generation as part of the business logic and store only the crux of the information.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in the post table, whatever URL you want to generate, keep that as part of business logic.

statement: In the image upload flow (prepare upload -> image upload service talks to S3 and generates a pre-signed URL -> client uploads to S3), the image service generates a random image ID; the post table should store just that random image ID instead of a URL.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if you just store the random image ID over here? URL, just the random image ID.

statement: Structure the way images are stored on S3 so that the path can be built on the fly: instead of dumping all images in the root folder, organise them per user, e.g. instaimages.com/<user_id>/<random_photo_id>, so all photos of a user sit in one folder.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you structure the way you are storing the images on S3 such that you can create the path on the fly.

statement: In the GitHub image upload demo, the upload key was '47-something' followed by the random ID; the 47-something was the teacher's GitHub user ID - GitHub organises uploads per user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What was that 47 something? That was my GitHub user ID.

statement: Given just the user ID and the image ID, the full image path can be generated, so there is no reason to store the bulky path - generate it on the fly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So why do you want to store this bulky part again over here? Can you not generate it on the fly?

statement: Generating the path at read time gives flexibility: from the stored parameters you can return a raw S3 path or a CDN path, change your CDN, A/B test CDNs, or use two CDNs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can generate raw S3 path, you can generate CDN path, you can change your CDN, you can do AB testing on CDN

statement: It is common that about once every two years senior management decides CDN costs are too high and asks to switch CDN or put 20% of traffic on another CDN; that is impossible to implement if the URL is stored, because you must provide that URL.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's switch the CDN. Let's put 20% traffic on other CDN.

statement: As a senior engineer you will face management deciding to switch CDN and cloud provider, and you have to work with that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's switch CDN and let's switch cloud provider. And you have to work with that.

statement: A stored S3 URL (instaimages.com/user_id/photo) cannot be served directly anyway; you would have to build the CDN URL on the fly by extracting the URL and doing string manipulation, so it is always better to store the crux information than the actual URL.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You anyway cannot serve S3 URL. You have to create CDN URL on the fly.

statement: Generate the URL on the fly in the API server: when reading a post, read the row, take the columns, create the (signed) URL in the API handler and send it in the JSON response.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Generate the URL on the fly, which means in the API server, when you're reading the post, you read the post, you read the row

statement: To move 20% of traffic to another CDN, the handler picks a random number: if it lies between 0 and 0.2 (20% of the time) it uses CDN A, otherwise CDN B - so you can compare the other CDN's performance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if your random number lies between 0, 0.2 or 20% of the times you generate, you use CDN A, otherwise you use CDN B.

statement: When Instagram migrated from Cloudflare to the Facebook CDN it would have done something similar; had it stored photo URLs it would have had to change every place and also handle where newly uploaded photos would be served from.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is how Instagram, when they would have migrated from Cloudflare to Facebook CDN, they would have done something similar.

statement: Deleting a user's image is easy with stored user ID and image ID: generate the S3 path and call S3 to delete it; with a stored CDN URL you do not know the S3 path and would have to trim the CDN part off - the worst way to build a system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: How will you delete something from S3 where you don't know the path?

statement: A post service handles the API calls to create/submit a post and to read a post.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Post service is where your API call to create a post, submit a post, read a post, that part would come over here.

statement: Upload-and-post flow: the user asks the image service to prepare an upload, which creates a signed URL on S3; the user uploads to S3 with it; once the upload completes, the client calls the post service, which creates an entry in the post database.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Once that upload is complete, it makes an API call to post service and post service creates an entry into this database.

statement: Separating images from posts is really important; the two are connected only through the image ID stored in the post, giving a clean separation of concerns instead of merging them.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So separating out image and post is really important. And the way they are connected is through this image ID in the post.

statement: Even though Instagram is 'all about images', today it is also videos, shorts, reels and stories - so you do not want to mix media handling into the post.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Today itself, Instagram is not just about images. It's about videos, shorts and reels and stories and this and that.

statement: With separation of concerns you can add an image upload service, a video upload service, a shorts/reels upload service, while the concept of a post stays the same and does not have to change.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But then your concept of post remains the same. You don't have to change it. That's the beauty of having separation of concerns.

statement: Implementation details (the nitty-gritties) are what matter; drawing boxes is the easiest part - real engineers think about the implementation and specifics at every step.
detail: Repeated at 01:36:44 ('Drawing boxes, again, as I say, is the easiest thing to do. Build things how they're supposed to be. How real world builds them') and at 01:39:08 ('that's not what real engineers do. Think about implementation. Think about the specifics. That's what makes you better').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: As I always say, my two year old daughter can draw these boxes, but what happens? This nitty gritties, these are important, right?

statement: Images are served through the CDN, which sits transparently between the user and S3; the AWS keys are uploaded to the CDN so it can read from S3 when the bucket is private.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDN transparently sits between your user and your S3. AWS keys uploaded on the CDN for it to read from S3 if it is private.

statement: Overall flow: user A uploads a photo via the image upload service, then posts it (an entry in the post table); user B visits A's profile and calls an API like /user/A/posts to get all of A's posts.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: user A uploads photo using image upload service. User A posts the photo, creates an entry into the post table.

statement: When user B's request reaches the post service, it selects the posts where user_id = A and builds the response with user ID and caption, but instead of the image ID it returns a URL (e.g. instacdn.net/a/12345) that the backend generates dynamically in business logic - possibly according to a CDN experiment - rather than storing it.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It is dynamically generated by backend. And that's really important.

statement: The frontend puts the returned URL in an IMG tag (or the image view on Android/iOS), which makes a GET request to it; the backend builds that CDN URL just by concatenating the fixed CDN prefix, the user ID, the random image ID and .png.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You have user ID, you have random image ID, .png, you concatenate them and you send it in the response.

statement: The IMG request goes to the CDN (instacdn.net); if the CDN has the image it returns it, otherwise it reads it from S3, caches it and sends it back to the user.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In case it does not have the data, it would go to S3, read the data, cache it and send it back to the user.

statement: Because the backend generates the URL, you can later add another CDN (e.g. Cloudflare) and have the backend generate cloudflare.cdn.net/a/abc.png for some requests, balancing between two CDNs seamlessly - this is why you never store the derived value.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So now you can balance between the two CDN seamlessly. Right. This is why you never store the derived value.

statement: Covered so far for the image upload service: storage, data flow, separation of concerns; next is privacy, the 'elephant in the room' for Instagram and most social platforms.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now what next? We covered storage, we covered data flow, we covered separation of concerns.

statement: Once something is out on the internet there is no privacy: even 'private' Instagram posts are not private, and the teacher says he can access them.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When something is out on the internet, it is out on the internet. There is nothing called privacy. Literally nothing.

statement: Even for a private account whose photos user B is allowed to see, the photos are still served via the CDN, because serving them directly from your own service would make costs shoot really high; you always serve via CDN for the best user experience, which means the photo is cached on the CDN.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you don't serve it via CDN and let you direct your service, then your cost would shoot really high.

statement: If a photo is on the CDN, anyone who has its URL can access it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if your photo is on the CDN, anyone having the URL should be able to access the photo. And that's what happens.

statement: Access by URL lasts only while the cached photo's TTL / certificate is valid; once the TTL or certificate expires the URL is invalidated and no one can access it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Once the TTL expires, once the certificate expires, then your photo becomes invalidated. Then no one can access it.

statement: If your profile is private and a follower uses inspect element to copy a photo URL and sends it to a friend who does not follow you, that friend can see the photo - so beware whom you grant access.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: one of your followers did an inspect element, copy it to URL and send it to other friend who does not follow you

statement: Browser dev tools (Chrome dev tools; the teacher uses Firefox's) are your best friend for seeing how real systems work.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you would have already known that your best is Chrome dev tools or whatever.

statement: Live demo: on his own Instagram profile, confirmed private by the class, the teacher inspected a photo, copied its image URL and pasted it into an incognito window - the image opened: 'privacy is a myth'.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But if I copy this URL and I paste it over here, tada, privacy is a myth, my friend.

statement: An Instagram image URL consists of the CDN domain (fbcdn.net - Instagram migrated from Cloudflare to FBCDN after the acquisition), a CDN path, the image name (a combination including the random ID) and a set of query parameters; the query parameters are what make the photos private.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Then you see a bunch of query parameters. This query parameters is what makes the photos private.

statement: A CDN has no authentication of its own and is 100% stateless: it does not know that you are user B, that you follow user A and are therefore allowed to see A's photos.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDN does not have any authentication. CDN is 100% stateless

statement: Instead, CDN access relies on time-bounded certificates: the URL carries an expiration time and a certificate created over it so no one can change that time - that is how CDN 'authentication' works.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it relies on certificates, basically time bounded certificates, which you create, you create a certificate out of it to ensure that no one...

statement: In the Instagram URL, the parameter OE is most probably the expiry (the teacher's guess), OH is the hash, there is an IG cache key (Instagram cache key) and an 'EDN' certificate-like parameter; these internal parameters are specific to the Facebook CDN, but every CDN has something like this - pick your favourite CDN and read its docs.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: OE, this is most probably the expiry. I don't know what this internal parameters are. It's very specific to Facebook CDN.

statement: Demo: removing some of these query parameters made the request fail with 'Bad URL timestamp' - a response generated by the CDN, which expected the expiry parameter (OE); with the parameters passed, the image loads.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But if I don't pass a bunch of these keys, right? It gives me error. Bad URL timestamp.

statement: Privacy is really enforced in the API server: viewers of a profile need the JSON response containing the photo URLs to render them; if the account is private and you do not follow it, the API server does not send that response at all. Only the API server can decide this, because only it has access to the database; the CDN never does.
detail: Repeated at 01:30:36: what matters is that the API service's /post call does not even return the response if the user is not following; still, anyone who has the photo URL can see it.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But when the account is private, I won't even send you the response.

statement: When a follower opens the teacher's Instagram profile they see his photos because the JSON response sends them the 15-20 photos he posted, each with its full FBCDN URL; for a private account that response is not sent, so nothing renders and the account shows as private.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because in the JSON response, I send you the 15, 20 photos that I posted. Right?

statement: This is pseudo privacy: companies only make it difficult for people to barge in, not 100% private - anyone with a photo URL can share it with friends who can view it until the key expires, and if a friend scrapes your photos and shares them your privacy is gone.
detail: 'It's no magic. It's just making it difficult for you to explore.'
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is pseudo privacy. They are just making it difficult for people to barge in.

statement: A truly private platform cannot use a CDN: every request - image upload, image download - must go through your API server, which checks on every request whether this user has access to read this particular image, because only the API server (with the database) knows who may read what.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So in case you want to implement a truly private platform, a truly private platform, then you cannot use CDN.

statement: Instagram cannot afford true privacy at its scale: routing every image request through API servers would need at least 50x to 100x more servers because of the huge image data transfer; it already runs a fleet of more than 100,000 servers.
detail: Hedged: 'That's what I've last heard. I'm not really sure. They keep on changing it.' He then says 'assume it's 100 servers. If it reaches 100 today, then tomorrow it would be 500 servers at least' (numbers as spoken).
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They would need at least 50 X to 100 X more servers. They are already running a fleet of more than 100,000 servers.

statement: Private CDN URLs use timed signatures, which work exactly like JWT: an expiration is baked into the URL's metadata and a certificate (signature) is attached so no one can change it; the CDN validates the certificate and checks the expiration time.
detail: If you are unaware of JWT, read about it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you are aware, it's exactly same as JWT. So you have an expiration baked into the metadata of the URL

statement: The CDN reads keys like OE/OH from the URL to find the expiry; if the expiry is, say, five minutes, requests arriving after five minutes are not served.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say that is five minutes. When the request comes beyond five minutes, then people would not be able to access it.

statement: The CDN maintains no state; it works only on such query parameters, and each CDN has its own set of supported query parameters.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now, depending on which CDN you use, they have their own set of query parameters, which they support.

statement: Signed-URL check: the URL is rendered via an IMG tag, the request goes to the CDN, the CDN extracts the query parameters, checks the certificate's validity and that the URL has not expired, and returns the image if valid, otherwise a bad-URL error.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It checks the validity of the certificate, sees if the URL is not expired. If not, it returns the image. Otherwise it returns bad URL.

statement: After storage, data flow, separation of concerns and privacy, the teacher only skims extensibility here because it is covered in great depth later.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now let's talk about extensibility. This is what I'll like skim through, extensibility, because we'll touch upon it in very depth.

statement: Kafka is the glue that stitches almost all social networks together.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Kafka is our friend. Kafka is the glue that stitches almost all social networks together.

statement: When a post is published, the post side pushes a message onto Kafka, which is consumed by multiple services - search, analytics, notification, feed and so on - each doing its own job.
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever the post is published, we push a message onto Kafka, consumed by multiple services

statement: With Kafka every consuming service can iterate at its own speed and pace; social media is all about extensibility, and Kafka is the central backbone connecting everything.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Kafka solves that problem for you, because now every service can iterate at their own speed, pace from this Kafka

statement: Kafka will be covered in much more depth throughout the course.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: like throughout this course, like Kafka will go very deep.

statement: Optimization is not about building a service on your own: building real-world systems means reusing things that already exist rather than reinventing the wheel every time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: building real world systems implies reusing things that already exist rather than reinventing the wheel every time.

statement: The class will build its own image optimization service tomorrow; today focuses on what the CDN gives out of the box.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll build image optimization service tomorrow. But today let's focus on what CDN gives you out of the box.

statement: Because a CDN's most common use case is serving images and videos, almost every CDN offers image optimization on the CDN itself, so you do not have to build that service yourself.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it gives you options to do image optimizations on the CDN itself.

statement: Why image optimization: not all users have high-speed bandwidth - if Sachin Tendulkar uploads a 50 MB photo and someone in a tier-3 city on Jio internet scrolls through 10 of his photos, their entire day's data is gone.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Imagine Sachin Tendulkar uploading photo 50 MB big.

statement: One way to optimize is to compress the image and prepare versions optimized for the resolutions of various devices.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You ensure that you compress the image. You optimize it for the resolution of the devices and whatnot.

statement: CDNs accept query parameters for image processing - just as they accept keys for privacy; one is the width parameter (W, width or OW depending on the CDN), the pixel width of the resulting photo.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDN accepts bunch of query parameters around image processing. One of them is a W parameter, or width.

statement: If a 10,000 x 10,000 pixel photo was uploaded and the user's device is only 360 pixels wide, there is no reason to send the full-size image to it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's say it uploaded 10,000 x 10,000 pixels photo. Hey, your user device is just 360 pixel big.

statement: The frontend, which knows the screen dimensions, appends a query parameter such as w=360 to the image URL it got from the backend before putting it in the IMG tag / DOM / image view - the frontend is smart now.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The frontend appends this new query parameter called w equal to 360.

statement: On a resize request the CDN first checks whether it already has the processed image path; if not, whether it has the original; if not, it fetches the original from the origin, applies the requested processing (w=360) on the CDN server, caches the result and serves it; later identical requests are served straight from the cached processed image.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it would do the image processing on the CDN server and cache it.

statement: CDNs can do much more image processing: resizing, colouring, grayscaling, transpose, rotation; some also provide recognition. Pick your favourite CDN and check its image processing capabilities.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Image resizing, image coloring, grayscaling, transpose, rotation. Some services also provide recognitions as well.

statement: Today you do not really need to build your own image upload/optimization service - the CDN gives the tools out of the box; you pay a bit of money and the problem is solved.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You just pay that bit of money. Problem solved.

statement: Recap of the image upload service: what a CDN does and the demo on the teacher's site; storage (chosen because it is cheap); data flow (uploading via API servers doubles the copy and needs 2x bandwidth, so upload directly to S3 via pre-signed URLs, with the GitHub demo); separation of concerns and not storing derived values; privacy (100% private only if everything goes through the API servers); extensibility via Kafka; optimization via CDN parameters.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Just to summarize, we first build an understanding of what CDN does.

statement: A student asked whether OTT platforms do authorization first and then grant CDN access; the teacher deferred OTT to the sixth week.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: OTT will talk later. We'll talk later. Sixth week.

statement: A student proposed protecting private images with a proprietary image format that only the Instagram app can open.
detail: Teacher: to render it, Instagram would have to ship the format's handling in its Android code; once it is out in the APK anyone can decompile and extract it - 'There is no rocket science.'
case_study: Instagram photo upload/serving is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Because for your Instagram to render it, they would have to ship it in the Android code.

statement: There is no such thing as a secure proprietary format: once you ship your code or jar, anyone can decompile it and reverse engineer the format - once it is out in public, it is public.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So there is nothing called proprietary format, because once you ship your code, ship your jar, you can, anyone can decompile

statement: DRM (as used e.g. by Udemy for videos) is very different from a proprietary format.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: DRM is different. Proprietary format is different.

statement: While building his platform the teacher implemented DRM, wore the hacker's hat and tried to hack his own system, fixing loopholes iteratively for 10 days straight; he can now catch who is doing mischief on his platform.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I wore the hacker's hat and tried to hack my own system, find out and kept on fixing it.
flags: check: "white hat" - repeats the student's phrase; maybe "black hat"

statement: Read more about DRM: the most interesting part is how the person who leaked content is caught, and that evidence acts as formal proof.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Read more about DRM. It's very interesting.

statement: According to the teacher, in India, if you pirate content and there is DRM proof that you did it, you go to jail for three years with no bail; laws are strict now and everything is traceable.
detail: Teacher: 'That's the statement from Indian government, FYI.'
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a DRM proof that you did it, you are in jail for three years, no questions asked.

statement: The teacher registered three formal piracy complaints in the last month; Google is also taking serious action.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In last one month, I registered three complaints.

statement: Images uploaded but never posted waste storage; since storage is dirt cheap it is fine to leave them, but if it is a concern you can find image entries in the database that have no post entry (not published) and clean them up.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can see the entries which are there but not posted, and you can clean it up.

statement: Kafka is used here because the other services must be told that a new post was published.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And you need to tell those service, right? A new post is published.

statement: The image service does not know which CDN node is nearest to a user - that is CDN-internal: the user fires a normal DNS resolution and the resolver resolves the domain to the nearest CDN IP address, which is done with the BGP protocol.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: User would fire a simple DNS resolution request, which is where the DNS resolver would resolve it to the nearest one.

statement: How CDNs route to the nearest node is not publicly disclosed: Cloudflare has a blog on it but calls it proprietary; only the CDN providers such as Akamai and Cloudflare know the actual details - the blog still gives a rough idea.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No one knows the actual details. Only Akamai, Cloudflare, the actual CDN providers know those details

statement: Akamai was the first to start this (CDN routing); Cloudflare hired a few people from Akamai - 'something around that has happened'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And Akamai was the first to start it. Cloudflare hired a few folks from Akamai to do it, but something around that has happened.

statement: A student asked how S3 locates an image when only the image ID is stored and the path is generated; the teacher: S3 is a black box accessed via the AWS SDK, just as the CDN is a black box for this system - that is the API contract, so we need not care where S3 stores it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: S3 is black box for us. For this system, S3 is black box. For this system, CDN is black box.

statement: After the break: the hashtag service - problem statement, brainstorming and low-level details.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll talk about again a very interesting service. We'll go down the details called hashtag service.

statement: Hashtag service problem: on Instagram, clicking a hashtag opens a page dedicated to it showing the hashtag, the number of photos, and (hypothetically) exactly the top 100 photos tagged with it; the goal is the best user experience when rendering this page.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: which contains the hashtag, the number of photos, and hypothetically, hypothetically, let's say we show exactly top 100 photos tagged with that particular hashtag.

statement: Assumptions: there are millions of hashtags, and a data science team's service generates the top 100 photos for a hashtag (trending, likes, comments, shares - their headache) and notifies us; it is a black box we do not build.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: assume that there is a service by data science team, how they bring up, but they notifies us whenever they generate top 100 photos

statement: Brainstorming for the hashtag service covers storage, large-volume counting, inter-service communication and, most importantly, super fast response time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We talk about storage. We talk about counting, large volume counting. We talk about inter-service communication and, more importantly, super fast response time.

statement: A student proposed a tags table (tag ID and name) and storing each photo's tags in the photos table.
detail: Teacher: the photos table is out of the question - think about the page you have to render; and the photos table has no special hashtag column, hashtags are part of the caption.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Photos table is out of question, right? You want to render this page.

statement: Design the storage from the page you must render: ask what you need to store in order to render this page.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now think on those lines. What are you storing in order to render this page?

statement: A student first proposed a tag table plus a key-value store (the teacher pointed out that is two databases), then one store keyed by the hashtag holding its metadata, incrementing the photo count whenever a photo with that tag is posted; the total photo count belongs there because it is exactly what the page renders.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: We can have one only then, like where we can store what is the tag key, and then we can store like values or the...
flags: check: speaker of "and by the way, why do you need it?" (Teacher? at 01:58:28)

statement: A student proposed maintaining the top-100 array themselves, updating it whenever an uploaded photo's popularity increases.
detail: Teacher: we don't have to care - we established the boundary that the data science team computes the top photos for us; do not assume otherwise.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: We don't have to care. That's what I said. Why are you assuming?

statement: The top 100 can be stored as an array in the same hashtag document; a student suggested photo URLs or post IDs, and the teacher chose post IDs (post ID 1, post ID 2, ...) - 'why photo URL?'.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Right? Why photo URL? Post ID one, post ID two and so on and so forth.

statement: Think through all possibilities before settling: if you do not consider the alternatives, whatever you thought of seems optimal but might not be.
detail: Arose when a student, asked for the advantage of storing post IDs, described how the data would be retrieved (joining with the post table) and admitted not having considered a second method.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If we don't think of all possibilities, whatever I think seems optimal, but it might not be.

statement: A student's answer on the advantage of storing post IDs: the post ID is data from which everything else (including the URL) can be derived, and it reduces the space needed for the hashtag document; the teacher accepted it.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So this, this way we can reduce the amount of space, that amount of space required to store this one document.

statement: For the top 100 you can either store the post IDs or store the actual post (the JSON response / the actual row) in the hashtag document.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you can either store the actual post, the JSON response, the actual row, the actual here, or you can store the post ID.

statement: Storing only image IDs in the top-100 list would be ambiguous because building the image path also needs the user; storing the post ID solves that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Post ID solves that problem.

statement: Copying the actual post object (ID, caption, whatever is in the post table) into the hashtag document is a denormalized way of storing things.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ID, caption, whatever we're storing in the post table, that same can be copied over, a denormalized way of storing things.

statement: Students noted the denormalized copy increases storage (teacher: correct) but means less data to fetch - everything comes in one go; the teacher: you just read this one document and send it to the user.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: You can just read this one document and send it to the user.

statement: A student pointed out that Instagram can show all photos for a hashtag; the teacher rejected extending the design: we are only doing the top 100.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: That's not just our top. We are just doing top 100.

statement: Do not add new requirements to the system mid-design - they require a different design; stick to the stated constraints.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Don't add new requirements to the system, because that requires different design, right?

statement: Approach 1 for the top 100: store only the post IDs (post ID 1, post ID 2, ...).
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: First way of storing this information is where we choose to only store the post IDs that are there.

statement: Advantage of storing post IDs: it needs less space, and because it is small it is very lightweight to cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The advantage of this approach is that we require less space to store the data.

statement: Disadvantage of storing post IDs: every render must first read the hashtag DB and then go to the post service/post DB for the details the UI needs (likes, comments, shares, caption, photo URL) - an extra database call.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you are making another call to a database, the post database, to get the detailed information about the post.

statement: Another advantage of storing post IDs: you always render the latest data, because every read goes to the post table, the source of truth.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the advantage of doing this is that you get the latest data

statement: Approach 2: store the actual post information (ID, caption and so on) in the hashtag document; it bloats the database, but with only 100 entries that may be fine.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This would bloat up this database. But given that there are only 100 entries, it might be just fine to do so.

statement: Approach 2 needs more space but gives very fast retrieval: read one document from one DB and return it, with no extra call to the post DB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You get very fast retrieval times, because you just have to go to this one DB, this one DB, read everything and return.

statement: Approach 2's problem is consistency: when a post changes (e.g. likes are added) the copies in the hashtag documents must be updated, which can become a pain point.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But another disadvantage of that is that if you do it, what about consistency?

statement: Depending on the guarantees you give, you might not show like and comment counts on the hashtag page at all - just the list of photos, tapping one opens the post page; then the simple denormalized approach works without worrying about consistency.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You might just want to show the list of photos, tapping on which you go to the post page. Very much possible.

statement: There is no single way to build such a system: which option you pick depends on the user experience and guarantees (SLAs) you provide - know the critical pros and cons.
detail: Also at 02:02:17: 'these are the critical pros and cons, because it's not just one way to do things ... depending on what experience we are providing our users, we have to know if we need the SLAs or not.'
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is no one way to build this system. It depends on the kind of things that you're providing.

statement: Each hashtag has an entry in the store; its total photo count must be updated every time a user posts a photo with that hashtag (count++).
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every time the user post a photo with a particular hashtag, you have to update this.

statement: A student proposed that the count does not need to be real time, so updates can be applied in batches; the teacher built on it.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I think it does not need to be real time. Correct. So we can have like the update to the service, like being added...
flags: check: "Correct." inside the student's own turn - may be the teacher

statement: The post service, where the post is made, pushes the post to Kafka.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is your post service where the post is made. You push it to Kafka.

statement: A student proposed a consumer that extracts the hashtags from each post, holds posts in memory for a while and commits aggregated counts - e.g. in a batch of 1000 posts, 10 with hashtag A, 10 with B, 20 with C - to the database.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I saw 10 posts with hashtag A, 10 posts with hashtag B, 20 post with hashtag C, and then commit them on the database.

statement: A student doubted hashtag as the Kafka partitioning key because there are so many hashtags.
detail: Teacher: the number of values is not the problem - the key just passes through the hash function, which picks a partition; the real problem is that one post has multiple hashtags.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Even if there are multiple values, then it's just, so it will pass to the hash function and pick one.

statement: Problem 1 with hashtag as the partitioning key of the post topic: one post carries multiple hashtags, so a post has no single hashtag key.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if you're taking hashtag as a partitioning key, there are multiple hashtags in the photos, in the post that you're publishing.

statement: Problem 2: the counting consumer must read the same Kafka topic the post service already publishes to on every post; otherwise the post service would have to write to two different Kafkas and the distributed consistency problem creeps in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Otherwise, this post service has to write to two different Kafka's and that distributed consistency problem creeps in.

statement: The post topic is partitioned by user ID or post ID - say user ID (the student's choice) - so all of a user's posts go to one partition.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What will be the partitioning key of this Kafka? Either user ID or post ID.

statement: For batching to work, all posts of a particular hashtag must reach one server; otherwise you cannot batch efficiently.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: All the posts of a particular hashtag should come to one server. Otherwise you will not efficiently batch.

statement: If three #sunset posts land on three different servers, there is nothing to batch and each server writes one at a time, so load is not reduced - the topic is partitioned by user ID but counting needs batching by hashtag.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is very inefficient, because this has to be parted by user ID, but this needs to be batched by hashtags.

statement: A student proposed Redis Pub/Sub with one channel per hashtag; the teacher rejected it: there are millions of hashtags, each cannot be a channel - it overkills the infra (massive, expensive) and risks data loss.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: There are millions and millions of hashtags. Each one cannot be a channel. You are overkilling the infra.

statement: If Redis goes down there is data loss, because Redis (Pub/Sub) does not persist anything - it is real-time Pub/Sub.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Plus, what if that Redis goes down? There is data loss, because Redis does not persist anything. It's real-time Pub/Sub.

statement: Hint example: the topic is partitioned by user ID, and post 31 is published with three hashtags: #sunset, #sun and #nature - how should it be routed?
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So post 31 is published: hashtag sunset, hashtag sun and hashtag nature.

statement: A student proposed that consumers of the user-ID topic parse each post's hashtags and write them into another Kafka partitioned by hashtag (a sharding-like idea), funneling each hashtag to one service with two Kafkas, similar to how a search index works; the teacher: that is exactly the point.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So in that way, you are basically funneling the hashtags into one service using two, what do you call it? Two Kafka

statement: Adapter: consume the user-ID-partitioned post messages, re-ingest them into another Kafka partitioned by hashtag, and reprocess there; a hashtag extractor reads the caption, extracts the hashtags and writes one message per hashtag into the new topic, which is consumed by a set of workers that write to the database.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: here you have to consume the message and re-ingest it in another Kafka and then reprocess it, something like this.

statement: With all posts of a hashtag on one server, the counter does count += n (n depending on the batch size) instead of count++ per post.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you don't want to do count++ but you have to do count++ equal to n.

statement: Partitioning by hashtag does not mean one partition per hashtag: it is hash-based partitioning (taught in week two) - the hashtag passes through a hash function and the value picks a partition, so e.g. three partitions can hold millions of hashtags.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: FYI, this does not mean we would have one partition for each hashtag. It's hash based partitioning that we discussed second week, right?

statement: Full counting path: the user-ID-partitioned topic is consumed by multiple hashtag-extractor consumers, which write one message per hashtag to the hashtag-partitioned topic; that is consumed by the counting service workers, which batch and update counts with count += n.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is your counting service. This takes care of counting.
flags: check: "all the posts of a particular user will go to one server" - likely means a particular hashtag

statement: Standard principle for large-volume counting: leverage batching. Without it you do count++ every time, causing a flood of micro writes that chokes the database and forces you to over-provision it; whenever you can batch, batch.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whenever you are counting something in huge quantities, what you have to ensure is you are leveraging batching.

statement: Instead of firing 100 separate insert statements you can send one batch/bulk insert of 100 rows; a bulk insert is about 100x faster than inserting one at a time - the best way to get performance out of a database is to batch its writes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Bulk insert is 100x faster than single doing that insert one at a time.

statement: This is a standard adapter pattern, found only by going into granular implementation details: the first instinct is to partition by hashtag, but you cannot change the standard post topic because search, analytics and notifications already consume it, so you add an adapter.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is a standard adapter pattern that I wanted to highlight.

statement: The compromise in this counting design: if some nodes go down, some posts may be counted multiple times; that is acceptable because an exact count is not needed - the page may show e.g. 1.2 million photos but renders only 100, and users will not check.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Here what we are compromising on, that in case some nodes go down, we might recount some things multiple times.

statement: You do not need strong consistency every time: at scale you can relax constraints, since some numbers here and there do not matter and there is always an error rate.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can relax some constraints when you are doing things at scale.

statement: For super fast response time, render the hashtag page in one shot with every piece of information in one document; if count, top-100 and other data came from different services, response time would grow. On a critical path do the bare minimum network I/O.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because you want to render this page in one shot, every single information needs to be there in one document.

statement: That is why the top 100 photos are stored in the hashtag database itself instead of calling the data science service at read time.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So that is why we are storing the top 100 photos in this database itself and not making a call to data science service

statement: A student started by defining the criteria for the top 100 (and then sorting posts by a metric value).
detail: Teacher: that is a black box for us - the data science team does it and we do not care how; we are the owner of this page only.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: black box for us, data science does it. We don't care how they do it.
flags: check: speaker - "We have changed the context" may still be DK

statement: A student proposed simply calling the data science service to get the top photos when needed.
detail: Teacher: we cannot call it - we have to store the data in our own database; the question is how they notify us that there is a new top 100.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: We cannot call it. We have to store the data over here.

statement: A student proposed a separate service listening to the data science notifications via a messaging queue and updating the store when a new batch for e.g. #sunset arrives, worrying it costs a constantly running service; the teacher: it is a simple processor - they give us the data in Kafka, we read it and update the store.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: the idea being that they give us this in Kafka, we read from it and we update it over here. Simple.

statement: A common mistake is to treat every consumer as a heavyweight 'service'; here it is just a process (a simple set of servers) whose job is to consume and update.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a lot of people I see make this mistake. Oh, service. It's not just a simple set of servers doing something.
flags: check: wording "It's not just a simple set of servers" reads opposite to the intended point

statement: Top-100 ingestion: whenever the data science service generates the top photos for a hashtag, it pushes an event onto Kafka (the best place for such notifications); we consume the event, get the top 100 post IDs and update them in the hashtag database.
case_study: Instagram hashtag page (hashtag service) is the running example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever the data science service does something, the push an event onto Kafka, we consume that event, basically getting the top hundred post IDs

statement: Why consume asynchronously instead of calling their service on each read: a synchronous dependency makes our uptime depend on theirs, so model things asynchronously wherever possible.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because then uptime of our service depends on the uptime of their service, because of synchronous dependency.

statement: Kafka is the glue that joins multiple services together, and this ability is why Kafka became widely famous.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And here we very beautifully see how Kafka becomes the glue that joins these multiple services together.

statement: The CQRS pattern exists because of this ability of Kafka to connect services asynchronously; it makes things neat.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The CQRS pattern that you might have heard of is because of this.
